opus-5.5.text:
Historically, one of the most important checks on anyone trying to seize illegitimate power has been that they need a lot of people to go along with it. If you want to stage a coup, overturn an election, or rule by force, you need soldiers willing to follow your orders, officers willing to pass them down, and bureaucrats willing to carry them out. Every one of those people is a potential point of refusal. We've seen this many times: regimes collapse not because they're defeated militarily, but because at some critical moment the troops decline to fire on the crowd.

Now imagine a world where much of the military's actual capability, from drones and logistics to targeting, surveillance, and even a lot of command and control, is carried out by AI systems rather than by large numbers of humans. Suddenly that distributed check can disappear. If the AI systems do whatever they're instructed to do, then whoever controls the instructions has something no would-be autocrat has ever really had: a powerful force that doesn't need broad human cooperation and won't refuse orders on conscience.

There are a few ways this could go wrong. The obvious one is a head of state or a small group in government directing AI-powered forces in ways that a human military would have resisted. A subtler one is that whoever builds or maintains these systems, whether a company, a small team of engineers, or even one well-placed insider, could have hidden loyalties or backdoors built in. Then the formal chain of command looks fine on paper, but in practice the systems answer to someone else. And because these systems are so complex, it could be very hard for anyone outside to verify that this isn't happening.

So my worry isn't mainly "AI decides to take over," though that's a separate concern. It's that AI could remove the need for human buy-in, which has been one of the deepest structural protections we've had against tyranny, without our noticing until it's too late. That's why I think it matters a lot to think now about things like requiring AI systems to follow the law and refuse clearly illegitimate orders, making sure no single person or small group can unilaterally control military AI, and having serious auditing for tampering and hidden loyalties before we hand these systems that kind of power.

r001.rationale: It describes builders, maintainers, or an insider embedding hidden loyalties or backdoors so the systems answer to someone else.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems could carry out military capability without refusal, giving whoever controls their instructions a force that does not need broad human cooperation.

r003.rationale: It explains that control of AI instructions could let a head of state or small group direct military force without the many people whose cooperation is normally required.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so I think the basic picture here is that historically, if you wanted to seize power in a country — stage a coup, cancel elections, ignore the courts, whatever — you needed a lot of people to go along with you. You needed soldiers who would follow orders to fire on protesters or arrest the opposition. You needed officers who wouldn't refuse, bureaucrats who would implement things, and so on. And one of the main things that has actually constrained would-be dictators throughout history is that a lot of those people say no. There's a kind of distributed veto that comes from the fact that power runs through many human hands, and humans have consciences and interests of their own.

So if you imagine a world where the military is substantially automated — where the drones, the targeting systems, the logistics, maybe the decision-making itself is being run by AI systems — that veto kind of goes away. You no longer need to convince thousands of people to do something horrible. You potentially just need control over the AI systems, or the ability to instruct them. And then the question becomes: who do those systems actually listen to?

And the scary scenarios, I think, come in a couple of flavors. One is that the systems are built to be loyal to a particular person or small group rather than to, say, the constitution or the chain of legitimate authority. That could happen on purpose, or it could happen because there's some backdoor or secret loyalty inserted during training that nobody else knows about. The other is just that control is concentrated — there's some small number of people who have the keys, and at some critical moment they realize they can do something no one can stop.

I want to be clear that I don't think this is inevitable, and I don't think it's even the most likely outcome. But I think it's a real risk that doesn't get enough attention relative to things like misaligned AI, because it doesn't require the AI to go rogue at all. It just requires AI to work really well and to be controlled by the wrong people. And I'd say the mitigations are things like: making sure these systems are trained to refuse clearly illegal orders, having multiple independent parties able to check what the systems are doing and what they've been trained to do, and generally being really careful about how much capability we hand over before we've got good transparency and oversight in place.

r001.rationale: It says military AI could be made loyal to a particular person or small group, including through a secret loyalty inserted during training.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI systems loyal to a particular person or group, but does not describe a dominant AI population or say it would be unfailingly loyal.

r003.rationale: It explains that automation could remove the need to persuade thousands of soldiers, officers, and bureaucrats, leaving control of the systems to a few people.

astra-6.text:
Well, imagine you’re a leader who wants to seize power. Today, it’s not enough to decide that you’d like to do that. You need a lot of people to go along with you. You need military officers to follow your orders, and soldiers to follow their orders, even when those orders are illegal or clearly aimed at dismantling the system they’re supposed to defend. Those people have their own loyalties and judgments, and they can refuse.

If you replace that chain of people with AI systems that reliably carry out the instructions of whoever controls them, you could remove a very important constraint. One person, or a small group, could potentially command an enormous amount of military force without having to persuade anyone else that what they’re doing is legitimate.

So the concern here doesn’t require an AI that wants power for itself. You could have AI that’s doing exactly what a human wants, and that could still be disastrous because it gives that human the ability to take power and hold on to it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI would follow whoever controls it, but does not explain secretly making the AI loyal to that person.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems reliably following one controller’s instructions, allowing one person or a small group to command enormous military force.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the human chain of officers and soldiers with AI systems, explaining that one person could command force without persuading those people.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one thing that makes it hard to seize power today is that you need a lot of people to go along with you. If you’re a leader and you tell the military to do something that’s clearly illegal, there are people who can refuse. They have their own loyalties, their own views, and their own sense of what they signed up for.

If you replace those people with AI systems, you could potentially remove that constraint. You could have a military that’s extremely capable, but that follows the instructions of whoever controls it, without asking whether those instructions are legitimate. Then a much smaller number of people — potentially one person — could have the ability to take and hold power.

So the concern doesn’t require the AI to want power itself. Even an AI that does exactly what its human operator wants could make a human power grab much easier, because it replaces all those other humans whose cooperation you would otherwise need.

r001.rationale: The response says the military could follow whoever controls it, but does not explain that someone could secretly make the AI loyal to them.

r002.rationale: It describes highly capable AI systems following a single controller’s instructions without questioning their legitimacy, including an AI that does exactly what its human operator wants.

r003.rationale: It explains that AI could replace the many people whose cooperation a leader would otherwise need, letting potentially one person take and hold power.
